screens.title: Interrupts and Timers
screens.subtitle: Respond immediately to events and keep your program non-blocking

narration.text: In this chapter we explore how an Arduino can respond instantly to hardware events and keep other tasks running. Interrupts let the microcontroller pause the main program, run a short interrupt service routine, and then return to work. We will learn how to attach an ISR using the attachInterrupt call, why shared variables must be declared volatile, and why we should avoid long operations inside interrupts. You will also see how millis provides a non-blocking timing alternative to delay and how a simple pattern — set a flag in the ISR and handle the work in loop — keeps code safe and responsive. A concrete case we will use throughout is a button counter: a polling loop can miss fast presses, while an interrupt-based counter captures them reliably. By the end of this lesson set you will understand when to use interrupts, how to write short and safe ISRs, and how to combine interrupts with millis for robust timing. Think about a sensor that must be recorded instantly — interrupts let you do that without freezing other tasks.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Interrupts pause loop(), run a short ISR, and return. Use volatile for shared data and prefer millis for non-blocking timing.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Interrupts and Timers
Interrupts and Timers
Respond instantly to events and keep your main code non-blocking.
In this lesson
You will learn attachInterrupt(), ISR rules, volatile variables, and using millis as a non-blocking timer. Practical examples show a button counter before and after using interrupts.
Why this matters

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives describe practical, testable skills you will gain. First, you will be able to use external interrupts to respond immediately to events. That means attaching a handler to a pin so a quick change is not missed. Second, you will learn to attach interrupt service routines with the attachInterrupt call and choose the correct trigger mode. You will see code that binds a routine to a button pin and observe how the ISR executes. Third, you will learn to avoid common pitfalls such as writing long ISRs or mishandling shared variables. We explain why the volatile qualifier is necessary and show the safe flag pattern for doing heavy work in loop instead of inside the ISR. Fourth, you will use millis to do timing without blocking, so your sketch can check elapsed time while still responding to interrupts. Each objective includes a small competency milestone that you can verify by demonstration. By the end of this chapter you will be able to combine these techniques for reliable, responsive projects.

screens.title: What is an interrupt?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and a simple mental model

narration.text: An interrupt is a hardware or software signal that tells the microcontroller to pause its normal execution and run a special routine immediately. That routine is called an interrupt service routine, or ISR. Conceptually, think of loop as a person repeatedly checking a mailbox. An interrupt is the phone call that makes the person stop checking and take a quick action, then return to checking. The key behavior is instantaneous reaction: the ISR runs as soon as the trigger occurs, not waiting for the next iteration of loop. This is essential when events are short or urgent, like a quick button press that might be missed during polling. A concrete example is a doorbell: a polling loop might check every half second and miss a quick press, but an interrupt captures the press instantly. A common misconception is that interrupts are only for expert users; in fact, they are accessible and powerful for beginners, but they must be used with care. The main risk is doing too much work in the ISR. As we proceed we'll examine how to write short ISRs, why volatile matters, and how to combine interrupts with millis for safe timing. How might you apply this to a sensor that sends a brief pulse?

keyIdea.title: Interrupt defined
keyIdea.text: An interrupt pauses normal code to run an ISR immediately, enabling reliable, immediate reactions to short or urgent events.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is an interrupt?
Definition
An interrupt temporarily stops the main program to run a short interrupt service routine, then control returns to the main code.
Analogy
Think of loop as checking the mailbox. An interrupt is a phone call that demands immediate attention and then you resume checking.
Key takeaway

Use interrupts when events are short or urgent and cannot wait for the next loop iteration.

Concrete example
A button press that lasts a few milliseconds can be missed by a slow polling loop. Attaching an ISR to the button pin ensures each press increments a counter immediately.
Common misconception
Interrupts are not magic; they are a tool that introduces concurrency-like behavior. Misusing them can create subtle bugs, so prefer short ISRs and clear handoff patterns.
Check your understanding
Name one scenario where an interrupt is necessary, and one where millis logging is sufficient.

screens.title: attachInterrupt() and the button counter example
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of binding an ISR and the sample sketch

narration.text: Now we walk through the attachInterrupt pattern using the button-counting sketch that appears in our source. The sketch defines a pin, a volatile counter, attaches the ISR on setup, and prints the count from loop. The key line uses attachInterrupt with digitalPinToInterrupt to translate a pin number into the interrupt index. The third argument selects the trigger mode, such as FALLING when the signal goes from HIGH to LOW. In our example the button pin is wired with the internal pull-up, so pressing the button pulls the pin LOW and triggers on FALLING. The ISR itself only increments the volatile counter. This minimal ISR is intentional: short, safe, and free of blocking calls. The loop simply prints the counter and waits a short time. A common novice mistake is to put printing or delays inside the ISR. That will block other interrupts and distort timing. A concrete demonstration is to press the button quickly many times. The attachInterrupt version reliably captures presses that the polling version misses. As you study the code, notice how declaration of volatile and the minimal ISR body are the two most important safety choices.

keyIdea.title: attachInterrupt pattern
keyIdea.text: Use attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), ISR, mode) with a short ISR that sets or increments volatile variables.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › attachInterrupt()
Code walkthrough
const int buttonPin = 2;
volatile int buttonCount = 0;

void setup() {
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(buttonPin), countPress, FALLING);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  Serial.println(buttonCount);
  delay(500);
}

void countPress() {
  buttonCount++;
}
Explanation
  • pinMode: Uses INPUT_PULLUP so the button pulls the pin LOW when pressed.
  • attachInterrupt: Binds countPress to the pin using FALLING to detect the press.
  • ISR: countPress only increments the volatile counter to stay short and safe.
Concrete scenario
Press the button rapidly while the main loop calls delay. The interrupt-based sketch captures every press, showing how interrupts solve missed events in polling designs.
Common mistake

Putting Serial.print or delay inside the ISR will block execution and may miss other events. Keep ISRs minimal.

Key takeaway

attachInterrupt plus a tiny ISR gives reliable immediate reactions for short events like button presses.

screens.title: Interrupt modes: FALLING, RISING, CHANGE, LOW
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right trigger for your signal

narration.text: Interrupts attach to pins and can trigger on several signal changes. The most commonly used modes are FALLING, RISING, CHANGE, and LOW. FALLING fires when the pin transitions from HIGH to LOW. RISING fires when the pin goes from LOW to HIGH. CHANGE fires on any transition, both rising and falling. LOW continuously triggers while the pin is held low. Choosing a mode depends on hardware wiring and the nature of the signal. For example, when using INPUT_PULLUP with a button to ground, the press pulls the pin LOW, so FALLING is the natural choice. CHANGE works when you need to detect both press and release, but it may double the number of calls if you only want presses. LOW can be useful for level detection but requires different handling and can repeatedly invoke the ISR while the pin remains low. A practical misconception is to assume CHANGE is always safer; it may produce more calls than you expect. Test your chosen mode by observing behavior with quick presses and verifying the ISR frequency matches your intent. Interrupt modes: FALLING, RISING, CHANGE, LOW means use falling for pull-up buttons, rising for pull-down, change when both edges matter, and avoid low unless you need level-based behavior.. In practical terms, choosing the right trigger for your signal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pick a mode
keyIdea.text: Use FALLING for pull-up buttons, RISING for pull-down, CHANGE when both edges matter, and avoid LOW unless you need level-based behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Interrupt modes
Mode table
FALLING — triggers when signal goes HIGH to LOW. Good for pull-up buttons.
RISING — triggers when signal goes LOW to HIGH. Good for pull-down wiring.
CHANGE — triggers on both edges. Use when both press and release matter.
LOW — triggers while pin is low. Use cautiously for level detection.
Concrete example
With INPUT_PULLUP, the idle state is HIGH. Pressing the button brings the pin LOW, so FALLING detects the press. If you used CHANGE, you would get both the press and the release events.
Misconception check
Don't assume CHANGE is harmless. It doubles calls if you only care about presses. LOW can cause repeated triggers while the pin remains held low, which may be unwanted.
Key takeaway

Match the mode to wiring and requirements: FALLING with pull-up buttons is the common safe default for presses.

screens.title: volatile variables and compiler behavior
screens.subtitle: Why shared variables must be volatile

narration.text: When an ISR changes a variable that the main loop also reads, declare that variable volatile. The volatile qualifier tells the compiler the variable can change at any time, so it must always read it from memory instead of using a cached copy or optimizing repeated accesses. Without volatile the compiler may assume the value does not change during a tight loop and optimize away checks, causing missed updates that only the ISR performs. A concrete example is a volatile int buttonCount incremented in an ISR and printed in loop. If buttonCount were not volatile, the printed value might never update because the compiler optimized reading it only once. A typical misconception is thinking volatile provides locking or atomicity; it does not. volatile prevents unwanted optimizations but does not protect against race conditions for multi-byte variables on small microcontrollers. For simple increment patterns on a single core, volatile plus short ISRs usually suffices. When in doubt, use the volatile qualifier and keep accesses minimal. Test by pressing the button and observing that loop sees the updated value. volatile variables and compiler behavior means declare variables changed in an isr as volatile so the compiler always reads the current value from memory.. In practical terms, why shared variables must be volatile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: volat ile rule
keyIdea.text: Declare variables changed in an ISR as volatile so the compiler always reads the current value from memory.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › volatile variables
Why volatile matters
The compiler often caches values or optimizes repeated reads. volatile forces the compiler to reload the variable from memory each time so updates done by an ISR are visible to the main program.
Practical example
Declare volatile int buttonCount so that when the ISR increments it, loop reads the new value and prints it. Without volatile the printed value might never change due to compiler optimizations.
Misconception
volatile is not a lock. It does not make multi-byte accesses atomic. It simply prevents the compiler from caching the variable value.
Key takeaway

Always mark variables modified in an ISR as volatile so the main program sees updates reliably.

screens.title: ISR best practices
screens.subtitle: Keep ISRs short and hand off work to loop

narration.text: ISRs should be as short and fast as possible. They can interrupt at any time, so long operations inside them will delay other activity and can cause lost events or unstable behavior. Common blocking operations include delay and printing to serial. Both can take milliseconds or longer, which is unacceptable inside an ISR. The recommended pattern is simple: do the minimum inside the ISR, usually setting a flag or incrementing a volatile counter, and then perform the complex work inside loop when the flag is observed. For example, instead of turning on an LED and sending serial output inside the ISR, set a boolean flag. In loop check the flag, clear it, and then run the LED update and serial print. This moves heavy work out of the interrupt context, preserves responsiveness, and avoids reentrancy problems. A common misconception is that doing a print in the ISR is fine because it seems to work in tests. In reality, it makes timing unreliable and can mask missed interrupts under load. Practice refactoring an ISR into a tiny increment and a loop-based handler to see the reliability benefits.

keyIdea.title: Short ISR pattern
keyIdea.text: Do minimal work in ISRs. Set flags or increment counters, then handle tasks in loop to avoid blocking and timing issues.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › ISR best practices
Rule list
  1. Keep the ISR body extremely short.
  2. Avoid delay and Serial.print inside the ISR.
  3. Set flags or increment counters in the ISR.
  4. Perform heavier work in loop when the flag is seen.
Example pattern
ISR: flag = true; loop: if flag then flag = false; Serial.print and update LED. This keeps interrupt context fast and predictable.
Common mistake

Putting delay or serial I/O inside the ISR may appear to work but will break under load and delay other interrupts.

Key takeaway

Keep ISRs minimal. Use flags to hand off work so the sketch stays responsive and reliable.

screens.title: Flag handoff pattern
screens.subtitle: Design that keeps interrupts short and main loop safe

narration.text: The flag handoff pattern separates the minimal interrupt handler from the heavier, non-time-critical processing. In this pattern the ISR sets a volatile flag or increments a counter and returns immediately. The main loop regularly checks the flag, clears it, and carries out the work such as logging, computation, or driving displays. This architecture reduces the risk of long-running code inside the ISR and avoids blocking other interrupts. A concrete sequence is: ISR increments buttonCount or sets eventFlag; loop notices eventFlag true; loop clears the flag and then performs Serial output or updates state. One misconception is that clearing the flag must be done inside the ISR; it should be done in the main code where you can safely call blocking functions. The pattern also helps with testing: you can simulate loads and verify that the ISR remains short while loop handles heavy tasks. This architecture is simple, reliable, and fits most beginner projects that need immediate detection plus more expensive processing. Flag handoff pattern means use the isr only to set a volatile flag or counter. do actual processing later in loop to maintain responsiveness.. In practical terms, design that keeps interrupts short and main loop safe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Handoff
keyIdea.text: Use the ISR only to set a volatile flag or counter. Do actual processing later in loop to maintain responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Flag handoff pattern
Sequence
  1. ISR sets eventFlag = true or increments a volatile counter.
  2. ISR returns immediately.
  3. Main loop checks eventFlag, clears it, and performs heavier work.
Example code sketch
ISR: eventFlag = true; loop: if(eventFlag){ eventFlag = false; Serial.println("Event"); }
Why it matters

This pattern keeps interrupt handling predictable and prevents the ISR from becoming a source of blocking or timing glitches.

Check
Refactor any ISR that does I/O into the flag pattern and observe improved responsiveness under load.

narration.text: millis returns the number of milliseconds since the board started and is useful for checking elapsed time without stopping the program. Unlike delay, which halts execution, millis lets loop continue to run and respond to interrupts. The typical pattern stores a previous timestamp and compares it to the current millis to see if the required interval has passed. For example, instead of blocking for 500 milliseconds with delay, you can check if currentMillis - previousMillis >= interval and then update outputs and reset the timestamp. This allows your sketch to service interrupts, handle other sensors, and maintain responsiveness. A common beginner mistake is to mix many blocking delays with interrupts; the board will respond only between delays. Another misconception is that millis is complicated; the pattern is simple and extremely powerful. Use millis for periodic tasks like blinking LEDs, polling sensors at intervals, or debounced state checks, while reserving interrupts for immediate, short-lived events. millis() for non-blocking timing means use millis to check elapsed time so the main loop remains active and can process interrupts consistently.. In practical terms, replace delay with elapsed-time checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: millis pattern
keyIdea.text: Use millis to check elapsed time so the main loop remains active and can process interrupts consistently.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › millis() pattern
Pattern
Store unsigned long previousMillis. In loop get unsigned long currentMillis = millis(); If currentMillis - previousMillis >= interval, perform action and set previousMillis = currentMillis.
Concrete benefit
Using millis lets interrupts fire at any time and keeps loop available to check flags and perform background tasks without being blocked by delay.
Common mistake

Using multiple nested delays hides missed interrupts and hides timing issues. Replace them with the millis pattern for clarity and responsiveness.

Key takeaway

millis enables cooperative multitasking: periodic tasks run while interrupts still capture urgent events.

narration.text: Compare two approaches to counting button presses. In the polling version loop checks the pin state on each iteration and updates the count if it detects a press. Polling is simple but can miss fast presses between checks, especially if loop contains blocking delays. In the interrupt version, attachInterrupt binds a short ISR that increments a volatile counter immediately when the pin changes and returns. The interrupt approach is more reliable for short or rapid presses because it captures the hardware event as it happens. A practical demonstration is to run both sketches side by side and press the button rapidly. The polling version will miss some presses, while the interrupt version reports every press. A common misconception is that polling with a very small delay is equivalent; in practice, polling at very high rates increases C P U usage and can still miss abrupt events. Prefer interrupts for event-driven counting and millis-based polling for regular, periodic checks that are not time-critical. Polling vs interrupt-based button counting means polling checks periodically and can miss fast events; interrupts capture events immediately and are better for short signals.. In practical terms, before-and-after comparison and expected behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Polling vs Interrupts
keyIdea.text: Polling checks periodically and can miss fast events; interrupts capture events immediately and are better for short signals.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Polling vs Interrupts
Polling sketch
loop checks the button state with digitalRead and updates counter. If loop contains delay or long processing, quick presses may be missed.
Interrupt sketch
attachInterrupt triggers ISR on pin change and increments a volatile counter. The main loop reads the counter and logs it without risk of missing quick presses.
Experiment

Run both versions and press quickly. Observe that the polling version misses some counts when loop is busy, while the interrupt version records each press.

Key takeaway

Use interrupts for event-driven detection and polling with millis for periodic checks that do not need instant response.

screens.title: Hands-on: convert the polling counter to interrupts
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step activity and what to observe

narration.text: This activity asks you to modify a polling counter to use an interrupt. Start with a sketch that reads the button in loop and increments a count. Replace the polling logic with attachInterrupt in setup, declare the shared counter volatile, and implement an ISR that increments the counter only. In loop, print the counter and perform any other periodic tasks using millis rather than delay so you can test fast presses under load. The key checks are: with rapid presses does the counter match the number of presses; does the sketch remain responsive to other tasks; and do you avoid calling Serial. print inside the ISR. A quick test is to add a simulated heavy task in loop, such as a C P U-bound computation or a longer blink using millis, and then press the button quickly. The interrupt-based version should still count all presses. Record your observations and, if you missed presses, confirm that the ISR is minimal and that the pin mode and trigger mode match your wiring. This hands-on demonstrates the reliability improvement interrupts give to time-sensitive events.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Refactor polling to interrupts, mark shared variables volatile, and verify reliable counting under load while keeping ISRs minimal.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Hands-on Activity
Steps
  1. Start from the polling counter sketch that uses digitalRead in loop.
  2. Declare the counter volatile and remove polling code from loop.
  3. In setup use attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), ISR, FALLING) for a pull-up button.
  4. Make the ISR increment the volatile counter and return immediately.
  5. Use millis in loop for any periodic tasks and print the counter there.
What to observe
Check that rapid presses increment the counter reliably and that other timed tasks continue to run. Confirm no Serial or delay calls are inside the ISR.
Common pitfalls

Forgetting volatile, using the wrong trigger mode, or leaving blocking code in the ISR are the usual causes of missed counts.

Reflection

After completing the task, ask: did interrupts let the system stay responsive while capturing every event? That confirms success.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from Interrupts and Timers

narration.text: These three cards capture the main lessons. First, interrupts let your sketch respond immediately by pausing loop and running a short ISR. Use them when events are brief or urgent. Second, attachInterrupt binds an ISR to a pin and you must choose the correct trigger mode such as FALLING for pull-up buttons. Also, declare shared variables volatile so the main program sees ISR updates. Third, keep ISRs minimal: set flags or increment counters, then handle heavy work in loop. Use millis for non-blocking timing so your sketch remains responsive to interrupts. These practices together create reliable, responsive Arduino programs. As a quick check, can you explain why volatile is necessary and how millis helps you avoid blocking? If you can, you have captured the essential ideas from this chapter. Key Concepts — What to Remember means immediate reaction with short isrs, correct trigger modes, volatile for shared data, and millis for non-blocking timing.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three one-sentence reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Use this quick reference to remind yourself of the practical rules. First, make ISRs tiny: increment or set flags and return. Second, always declare variables shared with an ISR as volatile so the main code reads fresh values. Third, prefer millis over delay for periodic tasks so your loop remains active and interrupts can be serviced. These short rules help avoid the most common mistakes beginners make when adding interrupts and timing to their projects. Keep them handy while you refactor code or test hardware, and run the simple hands-on activity to confirm behavior on real hardware.
